The bouncer is admiring an antiporter. An antiporter is a type of transmembrane protein that allows the simultaneous movement of two different molecules or ions in opposite directions.  The bouncer lets one person in for every two people that leave the club.  This means that for every 2 people moving in one direction, 1 person is moving in the opposite direction.  This is an example of antiport.  A uniporter is a type of transmembrane protein that allows the movement of a single molecule or ion across the membrane.  A symporter is a type of transmembrane protein that allows the simultaneous movement of two different molecules or ions in the same direction.  A GPCR is a type of transmembrane protein that allows the binding of a signal molecule from outside the cell to initiate a signal transduction cascade inside the cell.  This question was created using information from the PCS 3 lecture on membrane transport.

Virchow's triad is a set of three factors that are thought to contribute to the formation of a thrombus (blood clot) in the body. The three factors are:Alteration in the integrity of the vessel wall - this can occur due to damage to the endothelium, which exposes collagen and other sub-endothelial components of the vessel wall to the blood. This can lead to platelet adhesion and activation.Alteration in the composition of the blood to render it hyper-coagulative - this can occur due to the release of clotting factors, fibrinogen, or other pro-coagulant substances. This can lead to the formation of a clot.Blood flow - stasis of blood can lead to the formation of a clot. This is because the clotting factors and platelets have more time to interact and form a clot. The principles of Virchow's triad apply to the formation of a thrombus that causes a myocardial infarction. A thrombus forms on top of an atherosclerotic plaque that has ruptured. The rupture of the plaque can be caused by damage to the endothelium of the vessel wall. This exposes collagen and other sub-endothelial components of the vessel wall to the blood. This leads to platelet adhesion and activation. The platelets and other clotting factors then interact and form a clot. Blood flow is reduced due to the narrowing of the vessel due to the atherosclerotic plaque. This means that the clotting factors and platelets have more time to interact and form a clot. D is the correct answer! The first part of the immune system is the innate immune system. This is the first line of defence and is present at birth. It is the body's first response to a foreign invader and is non-specific. The cells involved are found in the blood and tissues. The cells are: found in blood = basophils, eosinophils, neutrophils, and monocytesfound in tissue = dendritic, macrophages, mast, and natural killer cells The second part of the immune system is the adaptive immune system. This is the second line of defence and is not present at birth. It is the body's response to a foreign invader after the innate immune system has been breached. It is specific to the foreign invader and takes 5-10 days to kick in. The cells involved are: found in blood = T cells and B cellsfound in tissue = dendritic and macrophages The third part of the immune system is immunological memory. This is the long-term response to a foreign invader. It is the body's ability to remember a previous exposure to a pathogen and respond to it more quickly and effectively if it is encountered again. The cells involved are: found in blood = memory B cells and memory T cellsfound in tissue = memory dendritic cells and memory macrophages

The correct answer is B - Urea. The development of symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, altered mental state and asterixis can be attributed to elevated levels of urea in the blood. This is a feature of Hepatic encephalopathy which is a manifestation of liver failure.  The urea in the blood crosses the blood brain barrier and causes the symptoms of encephalopathy.  The mechanism by which urea causes these symptoms is not fully understood but may be due to the fact that urea is an osmotic agent which draws water into brain cells causing cerebral oedema.  Other factors may also be involved in the development of encephalopathy, such as the presence of neurotoxins produced by bacteria which normally reside in the gut.  The gut barrier may also be compromised in liver failure allowing toxins to enter the circulation.  The other answers were made to test knowledge of other potential causes of these symptoms.  Elevated creatinine levels are a feature of renal failure.  Elevated potassium levels are a feature of various conditions including renal failure and diabetic ketoacidosis.  Elevated lactic acid levels are a feature of type 1 Lact acidosis which is a metabolic disorder.  Elevated calcium levels are a feature of hypercalcemia which can be caused by a variety of factors including primary hyperparathyroidism.

Calsequestrin is a calcium binding protein that is found in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) of muscle cells. It keeps Ca2+ locked in the SR and is only removed when the Ca2+ is released into the cytoplasm of the cell.  Calbindin is a calcium binding protein that is found in the smooth muscle of the airways. It keeps Ca2+ locked in the SR of the cell. It is removed when the Ca2+ is released into the cytoplasm of the cell.  Calmodulin is a calcium binding protein that is found in the cytoplasm of non-muscle cells. It binds to Ca2+ to allow muscle contraction.  Phospholamban is a calcium pump inhibitor. It inhibits SERCA and prevents Ca2+ from being pumped back into the SR. When phosphorylated it stops inhibiting SERCA and allows Ca2+ to be pumped back into the SR.  SERCA is the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase. It is a pump that moves Ca2+ from the cytoplasm into the SR.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes: responsible for phase 1 of drug metabolism, where the drug is modified directly by oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or de-halogenation. In the case of paracetamol, it is the cytochrome P450 enzymes that produce the toxic NAPBQI which is formed as a side metabolite in small amounts. However, in the case of a paracetamol overdose, the amount of NAPBQI produced is increased and it is highly toxic. Hepatic glutathione: In the normal case, the NAPBQI produced by the cytochrome P450 enzymes is conjugated and deactivated by hepatic glutathione. However, in the case of a paracetamol overdose, hepatic glutathione is depleted and so the NAPBQI produced is not deactivated and so has a free run of the nec. n-acetylcysteine (NAC): is a precursor of cysteine and is used in the treatment of paracetamol overdose as it increases hepatic glutathione levels and so deactivates the NAPBQI produced. n-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPBQI): is the toxic metabolite of paracetamol produced by the cytochrome P450 enzymes and it is the compound that causes liver necrosis in the event of a paracetamol overdose. UGT enzymes: responsible for phase 2 of drug metabolism, where the drug is conjugated to glucuronic acid, sulfate or glutathione to make it water soluble.
